newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine airport sale scaled back, but on course.
newsitem.headline: Argentine airport sale scaled back, but on course.

text.p: Argentina's airport privatization plans are still on schedule for mid-year, but the initial package of 59 airports up for grabs as concessions has been scaled back to a maximum of 25, officials and advisors say.
The government official in charge of the project, Alfonso Carlos Ensinck, rejected a recent press report that the sale could be postponed until 1998, telling Reuters:

"We should be ready to hand over operation of the airports to a concessionaire by mid-year. In principle it's 18 airports but some more provinces have expressed an interest, so in the first leg 22 to 25 airports should be involved."

The original project drawn up last year, which estimated the winners would have to invest $1.6 billion to bring Argentina's airfields up to scratch, did not take into account the autonomy of the provinces, which have to pass a law in their local legislatures before they can privatize.

Ensinck said the scaled-back concession would definitely include Ezeza international and Buenos Aires' domestic and short-hop airfield Aeroparque, and the airports of other major cities like Rosario, Mendoza and the ski resort of Bariloche. But he was unsure whether Crdoba, Argentina's second-biggest city, would be in a position to sell a private concession.

Argentina's Peronist government launched the airport plan last year and the bill was passed by the Senate in October. But its passage through the lower house of Congress has been delayed and there is now talk of a sell-off by decree.
"We are carrying out studies to see what would be the best way to implement it if we do not get a law (through Congress). It should be resolved in 10 to 15 days," said the official.

Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) is advising the government on the privatization. UBS vice-president of investment banking Michael Reynal told Reuters that President Carlos Menem has "stated very clearly he wants this done in August."

He described the interest of foreign airport operators in the sale as "huge" and said the scaling-back of the process from 59 airports should make it even more attractive. Under the latest plan, all the airports would be run by one bidder.

"With 59 airports, the potential concessionaires opposed the administrative burden. If you have less airports, it makes it more attractive," said Reynal, estimating this could push up the revenue to over the $1.5 billion the state expects.
Between 15 to 20 groups have expressed strong interest. They include:
- a German consortium led by Frankfurt Airport, with Thyssen AG and Siemens.
- an Italian group led by Rome and Milan airport operators.
- A French group led by Aeroports de Paris.
- A U.S. consortium led by International Airport Group.

- Aerosla, a group led by U.S. construction company Black and Veatch, the New York Port Authority and the operators of Schipol Airport in Amsterdam, which would build an island airport for Buenos Aires in the River Plate.
- plus bids from Spain, Ireland, Australia and Canada.

The concession would run for 25 to 30 years and include operation of runways, hangars and airport buildings as well as commercial activites such as shops, restaurants, duty-free and bonded warehouses.

La Nacin newspaper carried a report this week quoting unnamed officials saying one problem that could cause the sale to be postponed was that major duty-free and bonded warehouse concessions still have many years to run, and the government would face a stiff bill for compensation.
This is complicated by the fact that some concessions are believed to belong to a secretive local businessman alleged by ex-economy minister Domingo Cavallo to lead a crime syndicate.
Ensinck said the government has no intention of ending their contract early and paying compensation, so concessionaires would have to put up with existing terms until these expire in 2009 and 2010.

"It's clearly a contentious privatization and there are so many diverse interest groups," said one banker following the privatization process. "It's being used as a political tool in an already highly charged political year ahead of mid-term elections in Congress in October."
((-- Buenos Aires Newsroom +541 318-0695))
